messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Old Memories: Old photos, Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations, Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Kwame's Case

Kwame was twenty-two years old when he took the position of principal at Riverside Charter Academy, a decision that had seemed to vindicate everything he'd fought for since childhood. He was Ghanaian-American, raised by his father after his mother's death when Kwame was four. The early years had been marked by unpredictability—his father's moods shifting without warning, his discipline swift and severe. A forgotten homework assignment might go unnoticed one evening, then trigger a beating the next morning over something trivial. Kwame had learned to read the air in their home the way other children read picture books, always calculating, always braced.

By his teenage years, Kwame had channeled that hypervigilance into achievement. School became his refuge, then his identity. He excelled, went to college on a full scholarship, and had just completed his master's in educational leadership when Riverside offered him the principal role. At twenty-two, he was the youngest principal in the district. His girlfriend, Amara, had been proud of him. His father had said nothing, which Kwame had learned to interpret as approval.

The position itself felt solid at first—structured, hierarchical, a world of rules and expectations he could master. But three months in, Kwame began to notice something shifting. He'd be in his office reviewing staff evaluations when a teacher would knock on his door unannounced, and his chest would tighten. The unpredictability of it—not knowing when someone would need him, what they'd ask, whether he'd have the right answer—began to feel suffocating. He found himself snapping at administrative assistants over minor scheduling errors, then immediately terrified by his own anger, certain he was becoming his father. The fear of his own rage had become the dominant thought in his mind: *I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible.* He'd caught himself raising his voice at a teacher during a curriculum meeting and had left the room, hands shaking, convinced he was on the edge of something irreversible.

Around the same time, old photos had started to trigger him. His father had sent a box of childhood pictures—a gesture that might have been reconciliatory, though it was impossible to know. Kwame opened it alone in his apartment and saw himself at six, seven, eight years old, standing stiffly beside his father in various settings: a family reunion, a church service, a birthday party. In the photos, his own face was blank, watchful. He'd felt something crack open in his chest. That night, he'd had a nightmare—fragmented, senseless, but intensely vivid. He remembered the feeling of being pinned down, remembered a voice, but when he woke in a cold sweat at three in the morning, he couldn't piece together what had actually happened. The nightmare images felt more real than anything else in his life right now, more solid than his actual memories of his childhood, which remained frustratingly elusive. When he tried to deliberately recall specific incidents, the details scattered. He could feel the fear, the shock, the sense of being trapped, but the actual events remained blurred, as though they'd been photographed through frosted glass.

The nightmares had become routine. He'd wake gasping, and it would take him twenty minutes to remember where he was, that he was safe, that he was no longer a child. Amara had begun sleeping in the guest room. She'd tried to talk to him about it, but Kwame couldn't articulate what was happening. How could he explain that he felt permanently changed, fundamentally broken in a way that no amount of success could fix? He'd built a career, a relationship, a life of stability—and yet he was certain now that something essential in him had been damaged beyond repair. The worst part was the helplessness: the knowledge that no matter what he did, no matter how hard he worked to be different from his father, he couldn't stop the bad things from happening. They were inside him.

It was Amara who finally insisted he see someone. She'd found him in the bathroom at two in the morning, having called in sick to work for the third time that week, unable to face the unpredictability of the school day. She'd held his face in her hands and told him he needed help. Kwame had nodded, numb, and made the appointment the next morning. He was terrified of what a therapist might say, but more terrified of losing Amara, of becoming the man he'd spent his whole life running from.
